title: IEEE 1687: networks of instruments
summary: With hundreds of instruments, giving each one its own TAP instruction or putting all their registers in one long chain does not scale. **IEEE 1687 (IJTAG)** builds a reconfigurable **network** behind the TAP. This topic covers the network: the scan interface of an instrument, segment insertion bits, scan multiplexers, hierarchy and the link to the TAP. The next topic covers the languages ICL and PDL.
objectives: Explain why IJTAG networks are needed.
Name the signals of an instrument's IJTAG scan interface.
Explain how a SIB is built and how it changes the length of the scan path.
Design a hierarchical network and compute its path lengths.
Describe how the network is connected to the TAP.

items.title: One instruction per instrument?
items.md: Possible for a few instruments, but with hundreds the instruction register and its decoder grow, and every new instrument changes the TAP.

items.title: One long chain of all registers?
items.md: Simple, but every access shifts through **all** registers: 100 instruments with 40-bit registers mean 4000 bits for every read or write — even to change one bit.

items.title: IJTAG: a reconfigurable path
items.md: One TAP instruction connects the network. Inside, small switches decide which instrument registers are **in** the path right now. Only what is needed is shifted.

blocks.md: Every instrument in a 1687 network is reached through a **TDR** with a small, fixed set of signals — the same ones the TAP sends to its own registers (Topic 2). Any register that speaks this interface can be plugged into any network.

blocks.title: The instrument itself is not standardised
blocks.md: IEEE 1687 standardises the **access** — the registers, the network and how they are described — not what the instrument does. An MBIST controller, a sensor and a PLL all look the same to the network: a TDR with these ports.

steps.title: All closed
steps.md: Each **SIB** (segment insertion bit) is a one-bit register on the path. Closed, it adds only itself: the whole network is 3 bits long.

steps.title: Open one
steps.md: Writing 1 into SIB 2 (and updating) **inserts** the MBIST 2 register into the path for the next scan: 3 + 32 = 35 bits.

steps.title: Open others
steps.md: Any combination can be opened. SIBs can be nested, building a **hierarchy**: open a SIB for a whole core, then a SIB inside it for one instrument.

blocks.md: How is a SIB built? There is no special SIB primitive in the standard — it is made from two ordinary network elements: a **1-bit scan register (SR)** and a **ScanMux** that SR controls. The segment hangs between the ports *toSI* and *fromSO*.

blocks.caption: A SIB is a 1-bit ScanRegister plus a ScanMux selected by it

items.title: Hierarchy follows the design
items.md: Each core gets a SIB at the top level; instruments inside the core sit behind further SIBs. Opening a path is done step by step: one scan opens the core's SIB, the next opens the instrument's SIB.

items.title: ScanMux beyond SIBs
items.md: A ScanMux can also select between **different** segments — for example a short status register or a long diagnosis register of the same MBIST controller — controlled by a bit in another register.

items.title: Plug and play
items.md: Because every segment uses the same interface and is described in ICL, a core with its network can be reused in another chip; the tools rebuild the chip-level paths automatically.

subsections.title: Connecting the network to the TAP

blocks.md:
The network needs an entry point. Usually a TAP **instruction** connects the network's top-level scan input and output between TDI and TDO; the TAP's capture/shift/update states drive the network's enables. In ICL this connection is described by an **AccessLink**.

Other entry points are possible: the network can be reached through an IEEE 1500 wrapper, or from **inside** the chip — a processor or a test controller drives the same signals through an on-chip bus. That is how software runs instruments in the field.

blocks.title: One network, many access paths
blocks.md: Because the network is described once in ICL, the tools can generate access sequences for the tester (through the TAP) and for on-chip software (through the bus) from the same description.

questions.text: What does a segment insertion bit (SIB) do?
options: Includes or skips a segment of the scan path, depending on its value

questions.text: A network has 4 SIBs in a row. Behind SIB 3 there is a 24-bit register. SIB 3 is opened. How long is the path?
Why are IJTAG networks built hierarchically?
options: To keep the shifted path short and the access time low

questions.text: Which ports belong to the scan interface of an IJTAG instrument TDR? Select **all** correct answers.

questions.text: A top level has 3 SIBs. Behind one of them are 4 SIBs, and behind one of those a 20-bit TDR. Both are opened. How long is the path?
What connects the IJTAG network to the chip's TAP?
options: A TAP instruction that puts the network between TDI and TDO (AccessLink in ICL)
